passage: I work at the next desk to Sumit, so I saw this unfold. In March, Sumit's mother Urmila called every night from home, and one evening Sumit put the phone down and rubbed both eyes. "She wants me to quit and move back," Sumit said. "She says it's my responsibility. I love her. I also just got this promotion." I didn't know what to say. A week later Sumit brought a piece of paper to lunch: the mother would spend half the year with Sumit's aunt, and half in Pune with Sumit; a neighbour would drop in daily, and Sumit would go home once a month. "I told her honestly what I can and can't do," Sumit said. I can't say how it felt for Sumit, but the calls after that got shorter and warmer.

qa.q: In which month did Urmila start calling every night?
What might Sumit be feeling about the mother's request, judging from Sumit's words?
qa.a: Love and pressure at once: Sumit says Sumit loves her but has just got a promotion, and rubbed both eyes after the call.

qa.q: What arrangement did Sumit work out, and why is it reasonable?
qa.a: The mother would spend half the year with the aunt and half in Pune with Sumit, a neighbour would drop in daily and Sumit would visit monthly, so it honours her needs and Sumit's life.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt when Sumit said honestly what Sumit could and couldn't do?
qa.a: Urmila may have been disappointed at first, but the plan still kept her cared for and close to Sumit. The calls after that got shorter and warmer, which suggests she felt reassured.

grounding: Shows a parent expecting the protagonist to give up job, city or plans and calling it duty, the protagonist feeling love and pressure, finding arrangements that honour both and speaking honestly about limits, seen by an observer.

passage:
Sumit, you think your father is the first one to call a son home? Listen to your Jatin tauji.

When I was twenty-six, I had a good job in Delhi and a girl I wanted to marry. Then my father's eyes began to fail. He phoned and said, "A son's first duty is his father. Leave Delhi. Come back to Meerut." My mother cried in the background.

I felt pulled in half. I loved him. And I knew if I gave up everything I would resent him for the rest of his life.

So I went home one weekend and said it plainly. "Papa, I can't leave my job. But I can come every Saturday, I'll find someone to read to you in the afternoons, and I'll ask for a transfer to Ghaziabad." He sulked for a month. The transfer came the next spring. I married in December. He danced at my wedding.

qa.q: What did Jatin's father ask him to do when his eyes began to fail?
qa.a: He asked Jatin to leave Delhi and come back to Meerut.

qa.q: How did young Jatin feel when his father called?
qa.a: He felt pulled in half, loving his father but afraid he would resent him if he gave up everything.

qa.q: What choice in the story honoured both the father and Jatin's own life?
qa.a: Going home to speak plainly and offering weekly visits, a reader for the afternoons and a transfer closer, instead of quitting his job.

qa.q: How might Jatin's father have felt during the month he sulked?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and disappointed that his son did not simply obey, though he later came round and danced at the wedding.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man whose parent calls it his duty to give up his job, feeling love and pressure, who finds an arrangement that honours both and speaks honestly.

passage:
The offer letter from the Singapore office gave Zubin forty-eight hours to sign. He read it in the hospital canteen, where his mother was recovering from a knee replacement upstairs.

When he told her, she turned to the wall. "Your father left me alone for work. Now you. A son stays." The nurse came in to take her pressure and Zubin went out to the corridor, heart pounding. He loved her. He also wanted this job more than anything in years.

He spent the night making calls. His cousin Freny could move into the spare room. A day attendant could come from eight to six. He called the office and asked if the start could move by two months.

In the morning he sat by her bed. "Mamma, I'm going, but not yet, and not leaving you alone. I'll be here until you can walk to the market. Then I'll call daily and come every three months."

She didn't answer. But she held his hand.

qa.q: How long did the offer letter give Zubin to sign?
How did Zubin feel when his mother turned to the wall?
qa.a: Zubin felt torn and anxious, his heart pounding, loving her but wanting the job badly.

qa.q: How did Zubin try to honour both his mother's needs and his own life?
qa.a: He arranged a cousin and a day attendant, asked to delay his start, and told his mother honestly what he could and could not do.

qa.q: What might Zubin's mother be feeling when she holds his hand?
qa.a: She may feel afraid of being alone and hurt, yet reassured by his plan and his honesty.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose parent calls it his duty to give up a job abroad, feeling love and pressure, who finds an arrangement that honours both lives and speaks honestly about limits.
